events.title: PhD Dissertation Defense: Eliel Akinbami
events.description:
Title: Reading Enzyme Function from Sequence and Structure

Abstract: Enzymes are among the most proficient catalysts known – the bacterial phosphatase PafA, for example, accelerates its reaction by roughly 1027-fold relative to the uncatalyzed reaction. Yet how a linear amino-acid sequence folds into a structure that achieves this, and how mutations to individual residues tune catalytic activity, is still only partly understood. High-throughput platforms such as HT-MEK now measure the catalytic consequences of thousands of mutations in parallel, but these functional data reveal what mutant changes activity, rarely how or why. Here I use PafA as a model system to close part of that gap through two complementary studies. 

Initial PafA experiments revealed that some mutations far from the active site (i.e D473V) had surprisingly large impacts on substrate specificity. Here, I explain this finding by acquiring high-resolution (1.6 Å) cryo-EM structures that show PafA forms a tetrameric complex in which this distal residue is closer to the active site of the neighboring protomer. Combining structural and functional data further reveals D473V alters substrate specificity by changing the conformation of a substrate-contacting residue R164.

Second, I confront a neglected confounder present in many in vitro high-throughput measurements: misfolded proteins can dramatically distort measured kinetic constants, but most high-throughput assays do not test for or quantify misfolding. To address this, I developed deFOLD (Degradation Enabled Fraction folded of On-Bead Library Displays), a bead-based proteolysis assay that can quantify the misfolded fraction of thousands of variants at once, enabling corrected kinetic parameters and a direct, scalable readout of folding that most high-throughput methods lack.

events.title: Science-Based Strategies to Support Your Immune System
events.description:
The immune system is a remarkably complex network of organs, cells, and chemical messengers that protects us from infection every day. Yet we're constantly bombarded with products, remedies, and online advice claiming to "boost" immunity. How can you tell what's supported by science and what's simply marketing?

In this noontime webinar, you'll learn how the immune system works, how it changes as we age, and what lifestyle habits truly support immune health. We'll separate fact from fiction as we examine the evidence behind nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress management, supplements, and other popular immune remedies.

You'll also discover why vaccines work differently from remedies that claim to "boost" immunity, how they train the immune system to recognize specific threats, and why vaccination remains one of the most effective tools for preventing serious infectious diseases.

You'll leave with practical, evidence-based strategies you can use right away and a clearer understanding of what really supports a healthy immune system.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants. 

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.  

Request disability accommodations and access info.

Class details are subject to change.

events.title: Understanding Latin America’s Economy in the Twenty-first Century
events.description:
Latin America’s economic performance is often depicted as a long sequence of repeated failures, including its contribution to global financial crises as well as its slow growth and intractable inequalities. Its experience in the twenty-first century, however, reveals considerable and underappreciated successes (as well as setbacks). This talk will review the region's growth and development in the last quarter century, including the commodity boom, a surprising decline in economic inequality, responses to the financial and Covid-19 crises, and the emergence of left-leaning governments that opted for pragmatic and orthodox macro policies mixed with innovative antipoverty programs.

Livestream Link

Jeff Dayton-Johnson has served as vice president of academic affairs and dean at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey since 2014. He is also a professor of international policy & development there. Prior to joining MIIS, he was senior economist for Latin America & the Caribbean at the OECD Development Centre in Paris, and assistant and associate professor of economics and international development studies at Dalhousie University in Canada. Dayton-Johnson's research and teaching interests include economic development, inequality, Latin America & the Caribbean, public policy, migration, social cohesion. He earned a PhD in economics and an AB hons in Latin American Studies at UC Berkeley.

events.description:
[Podcast: This Week in Virology]

Increasing Participation of Spanish Speakers with Limited English Proficiency (LEP) in HIV Clinical Research in the U.S.

Latinx individuals account for nearly 30% of new HIV infections in the United States yet comprise less than 12% of participants in HIV clinical trials. To evaluate the structural mechanisms underlying this disparity, a qualitative needs assessment was conducted evaluating barriers, language access practices, and institutional frameworks across clinical research sites (CRSs) in the country affiliated with the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)-funded networks, including the HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN), HIV Prevention Trials Network (HPTN), and Adolescent Medicine Trials Network (ATN). This webinar will present the preliminary results of this research contrasting ideal federal aspirations—such as the revised NIH Policy and Guidelines on the Inclusion of Women and Minorities as Subjects in Clinical Research of July 2025, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) December 2025 Guidance on broadening eligibility criteria, and the statutory protections under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act—against the operational field realities reported by CRS’s research personnel.

Speakers:
Pedro Goicochea, MSc, MA is a public health independent researcher with decades of experience in communications, HIV prevention, clinical research, and community engagement across the United States and Latin America. Originally from Peru, he relocated to the U.S. in 2008 to contribute to the landmark iPrEx study—the first clinical trial to demonstrate the efficacy of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in preventing HIV among men and transgender women.
